title: Empirical Strategies in Labor Economics
research_question: How do schooling, union membership, immigration, military service, and class size causally affect labor market outcomes such as earnings, employment, and student achievement? More broadly, how can researchers credibly recover counterfactual outcomes when the variable of interest is not randomly assigned?
data_description: The chapter draws on numerous US micro datasets to illustrate empirical strategies, including the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, National Longitudinal Surveys, Current Population Survey, Survey of Economic Opportunity, decennial Census files (notably 1980 and 1990), the Survey of Income and Program Participation, and Social Security administrative earnings records. Key variables include log weekly or annual earnings, years of schooling, union status, veteran status, test scores, demographic characteristics (age, race, sex, state and quarter of birth), and class size. Sample periods span cohorts born in the 1930s through applicants to the all-volunteer military in 1979–1982 and Israeli fifth graders in 1991. Units of observation are typically individual workers, applicants, or pupils, sometimes aggregated to school or city-year cells (e.g., Miami and four comparison cities, 1970s–1990s establishment employment data).
institutional_context: The chapter motivates its examples with several concrete settings. US compulsory schooling laws permit students to leave school on their 16th birthday, so children born later in the calendar year complete more schooling because of the interaction between school-entry rules and dropout age. The Vietnam-era draft used randomized lottery numbers assigned to birth dates in 1970–1972 to determine conscription priority, while later cohorts faced an all-volunteer force that screened applicants on age, schooling, and AFQT scores. The 1980 Mariel Boatlift suddenly raised Miami's labor force by about 7% through Cuban immigration. Israeli public schools follow Maimonides' Rule, which caps class size at 40 pupils and mechanically splits grades once enrollment exceeds multiples of 40. Union coverage, government training programs (CETA, NSW), and financial aid awards provide additional policy settings.
